analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to send students a standardized, plain-language financial aid offer showing true costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2022 and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every college that takes federal student aid to give students a standardized financial aid offer with plain-language terms. The offer would have to separate direct costs like tuition from indirect costs like housing and food, state clearly what is a grant you don't repay versus a loan you do repay with interest, ban schools from labeling offers as "award letters," and show students typical earnings and loan payments for graduates of their program. The Department of Education would write the detailed rules after testing them with students, families, and schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Prospective and enrolled students and their families — especially first-generation, low-income, and veteran students — who today often receive confusing aid letters that lump grants and loans together or imply loans reduce costs. The bill would make the real price, the free aid, and the borrowed money visibly distinct before a student commits [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and families comparing college costs

how_it_helps.text: Requires every college in federal aid programs to use a standardized financial aid offer with common terms, definitions, and formatting, based on consumer testing with students and families [S2] [S3].

Prohibits offers from displaying loans in a way that implies they reduce the amount owed or out-of-pocket costs, and requires clear labels of subsidized versus unsubsidized loans and disclosures that grants need not be repaid while all loans must be repaid with interest [S3].

Separates direct costs (tuition and fees) from indirect costs (housing, food, books, transportation), shows out-of-pocket costs for each, and bars schools from calling the offer an "award letter" [S2] [S3].

Requires offers to disclose whether institutional grant aid will continue in later years or be reduced if outside scholarships arrive, and to show median graduate earnings and loan payments for the student's program [S3].
Directs the Department of Education to make College Scorecard and college websites publish cost, earnings, and loan payment information consistent with the standardized offer terms [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities bear the administrative cost of rebuilding their financial aid letters to meet the federal standard, testing them, and maintaining consistent data on their websites. Private student lenders and PLUS-loan-heavy financing paths could see fewer borrowers drift into them if federal loan terms are laid out more clearly. Tuition itself would not go down; students would see costs more clearly but pay the same prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill is disclosure-only: it standardizes what students are told but does nothing to lower tuition, fees, or loan balances, so a better-informed student still faces the same bill [S2] [S3].

Compliance would impose new administrative burdens on colleges, which must rework offers within a year of the Secretary's rules, run consumer-testing participation, and keep website cost and earnings data consistent with the standard terms — costs that fall hardest on small institutions [S3].

The bill requires disclosure that other financing options — including private education loans and Federal Direct PLUS loans — may be available, which could surface higher-cost borrowing options to students alongside the standardized terms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-targeted consumer protection. Its genuine benefit is real: today's aid letters routinely bury loan amounts among grants, and standardized plain-language offers with tested formatting would help families compare true prices. But it does not touch the underlying cost of college, and its costs to schools are administrative rather than financial pain. On balance the benefit to students outweighs the compliance burden, though it is a transparency fix, not an affordability fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last month of the Congress and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Lisa McClain of Michigan introduced the bill on December 5, 2022, with Representative Virginia Foxx joining as an original cosponsor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1] [S3] [S5].
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges are better off because the bill died: they keep full discretion over how they present aid offers, with no standardization, no ban on "award letter" language, and no requirement to separate grants from loans or disclose when their own grant aid can be reduced. Students continue to navigate whatever format each school chooses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges, which keep their current aid letters

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition: the bill had only Republican sponsorship (the sponsor, an original cosponsor, and two cosponsors in total, all R) [S4], and it died quietly in committee without any vote or floor debate to reveal a party split [S5].

industries.note: The bill would force every college receiving federal aid to replace its own aid-letter format with a standardized, consumer-tested offer that separates grants from loans and shows true out-of-pocket costs — a real compliance cost, especially for small schools. Schools lose the flexibility to present offers in ways that make loans look like free money, which is precisely the benefit to students.

The bill would require offers to disclose that private education loans and other financing options exist, but would also require federal loans to be clearly labeled and shown as repayable with interest, listed after cash payment. Clearer federal terms could steer some borrowers away from private loans, though the disclosure requirement also gives private lenders a named place in every offer.
